chapter.name: Grassroots Democracy - Part 1: Governance
chapter.blurb: Human societies need rules to function: governance is the process of making decisions and rules and ensuring they are followed, the government is the system that does this, and its most important rules are called laws. A government works through three separate organs -- the legislature, the executive and the judiciary -- which interact under a system of checks and balances, and it functions at three levels: local, State and Central. Fig. 10.5 sets out how the judiciary, legislature and executive are each structured at the national and State level, including the meaning of a 'nominal' head such as the President or a Governor. India, the world's largest democracy, is a representative democracy in which citizens elect MLAs and MPs to decide on their behalf, while grassroots democracy is the idea that ordinary citizens should also have a direct say in decisions that affect them.

scope_in.item: Define governance as the process of taking decisions, organising society's life through different sets of rules, and ensuring that the rules are followed; define government as the group of individuals or the system that makes the rules and ensures they are followed; define law as one of the more important rules a government makes; and understand that rules apply across many areas of life (home, school, examinations, traffic, and the workplace, for both employees and employers) and that citizens have a say in changing them

Name and describe the three organs of government -- the legislature (makes, updates or removes laws through an assembly of representatives), the executive (implements the laws; includes the head of state, ministers and law-enforcement agencies) and the judiciary (the system of courts that decides whether a law has been broken and what action should follow, and can also examine whether the executive or legislature acted fairly) -- illustrated through the chapter's cybercrime example

Explain the separation of powers: the three organs are kept separate although they interact and work together, providing a system of checks and balances in which each organ can check the others and restore balance if one oversteps its role

Name and describe the three levels/tiers at which a democratic government, including India's, operates -- local (town or village), State and Central/national/Union -- each dealing with different matters, using the bulb-repair and flood-response examples; identify the Government of India's motto (Satyameva Jayate) and the Supreme Court's motto (Yato Dharmastato Jayah)

Read Fig. 10.5's summary of the judiciary and legislature at the All India/national level and the State level: Supreme Court of India / High Court; and the Lok Sabha and Rajya Sabha (which formulate national laws) / one State Assembly or Vidhan Sabha (most States have a single assembly, a few have two); know the glossary meaning of 'House'

Read Fig. 10.5's summary of the executive at the Central and State level: the President (nominal head, Supreme Commander of the Indian Armed Forces) and Prime Minister / the Governor (nominal head) and Chief Minister; know the glossary meaning of 'nominal'; read the (non-exhaustive) lists of Central and State executive functions, noting Education appears in both; and use Dr. A.P.J. Abdul Kalam's example (11th President, 2002-2007) to show that a nominal head can still have real, positive influence

Explain the meaning of democracy (Greek 'demos' = people, 'kratos' = rule/power); explain that India is a representative democracy in which citizens elect MLAs (State level) and MPs (national level); distinguish direct democracy (the class-picnic voting example) from representative democracy (the class-monitor example); state that India is the world's largest democracy (about 970 million voters in 2024, voting age 18); and define grassroots democracy as enabling ordinary citizens' participation, the base of the three-tier pyramid

concepts.name: Governance, government and law
concepts.description: Societies need rules to function; governance is the process of making and enforcing them, government is the system that does so, and laws are its most important rules.
concepts.idea: When many people live together, rules become necessary to maintain order and harmony; governance is the process of taking decisions, organising society's life with rules, and ensuring the rules are followed.
concepts.rule: The group of individuals or the system that makes the rules and ensures they are followed is called a government; some of the more important rules made by a government are called laws; and rules and laws are not fixed forever -- citizens can have a say in changing them, just as a student body might ask a school to change a rule.
concepts.example: Rules exist at home, in school (for both students and teachers), for students appearing for examinations, for drivers on the road (traffic rules), and for employees and employers alike; without such rules, the chapter says, 'society would not be able to function'.

concepts.name: The three organs of government
concepts.description: A government works through three organs -- the legislature, the executive and the judiciary -- kept separate but working together under a system of checks and balances.
concepts.idea: The legislature is the organ that makes (or 'legislates'), updates or removes laws, through an assembly of representatives; the executive is the organ that implements the laws, including the head of state, the ministers and any law-enforcement agency; the judiciary is the system of courts that decides whether a law has been broken and what action should follow, and can also examine whether the executive or legislature acted fairly.
concepts.rule: In good governance the three organs are kept separate, although they interact and work together -- this is called the 'separation of powers'. It provides a system of checks and balances, so each organ can check what the others are doing and restore balance if one oversteps its role.
concepts.example: When cybercriminals steal money digitally, the legislature passes laws against cybercrime, the executive (through the cyber police) enforces them and investigates, and the judiciary tries the accused in court and decides their punishment -- showing all three organs at work together.

questions.q: Using the chapter's cybercrime example, explain step by step how the legislature, the executive and the judiciary each play a distinct role in dealing with a cybercriminal, from the crime being committed to the punishment being decided.
questions.a: First, the legislature passes new laws to fight cybercrime, since these criminals use new digital methods to steal money. Next, the executive -- through an enforcement agency such as the cyber police -- investigates the crime and arrests the criminal under these laws. Finally, the judiciary tries the accused in court, decides whether the law has been broken, and if so, decides on the punishment, such as a fine and a jail term. Each organ plays a distinct, necessary role in the same process.

questions.q: The chapter asks readers to imagine the disorder that might result if all three organs of government were under the control of the same group of people. Using the chapter's own explanation of checks and balances, explain why this would cause disorder.
questions.a: If the same group controlled all three organs, there would be no separate organ left to check whether that group's laws, actions or decisions were fair or lawful. The whole point of checks and balances is that each organ can check what the others are doing and restore balance if one oversteps its role; with only one group in control of all three, this checking would disappear, and the group's power would go unchecked.
s: Explains that with one group controlling all three organs, no organ remains to check the others

questions.q: A student argues, 'Since the executive enforces the law and the judiciary punishes lawbreakers, the legislature is the least important of the three organs.' Evaluate this claim using the chapter's cybercrime example.
questions.a: This claim is not well supported. In the chapter's cybercrime example, the legislature's role -- passing new laws to fight cybercrime -- comes first and makes the other two organs' work possible: without a law against cybercrime, the executive would have no legal basis to arrest offenders, and the judiciary would have no law to try them against. All three organs depend on each other and play necessary, connected roles; the chapter itself frames this as the three organs 'working together', not one being more or less important than the others.
s: Rejects or substantially qualifies the claim rather than accepting it outright

concepts.name: The three levels of government
concepts.description: A democratic government, including India's, works at three levels -- local, State and Central -- each dealing with different matters depending on their scale.
concepts.idea: Any democratic government operates at multiple levels; in India, as in many countries, it functions at three levels or tiers -- local (town or village), State (regional) and national (Central or Union) -- and each level deals with different matters.
concepts.rule: Problems are generally handled by the level of government best suited to their scale: local matters by local government, State-wide matters by the State Government, and matters affecting the whole nation by the Central Government -- with higher levels stepping in only when a lower level cannot cope alone.
concepts.example: If a household's bulb is not lighting up, one first checks the bulb, switch and fuse, then calls an electrician, and only escalates to the Electricity Board if the problem lies beyond the home; similarly, a small flood is handled by local authorities, a larger one brings in the State Government, and a massive flood affecting vast areas brings in the Central Government (with the army and relief supplies).

concepts.description: Fig. 10.5 also sets out the executive's leadership and functions at the Central and State level, including the meaning of a 'nominal' head.
concepts.idea: The Central Government's executive is led by the President of India (the nominal head and Supreme Commander of the Indian Armed Forces), with the Prime Minister as the executive head; the State Government's executive is led by the Governor (the nominal head), with the Chief Minister as the executive head. concepts.example: Dr. A.P.J. Abdul Kalam, the 11th President of India (2002-2007), shows that even though the President's position is nominal, he still played an important role and impacted countless lives through his dedication to education and youth.

concepts.name: Democracy, representative democracy and grassroots democracy
concepts.description: Democracy means 'rule of the people'; India is a representative democracy where elected MLAs and MPs decide on citizens' behalf, and grassroots democracy is about ordinary citizens having a say.
concepts.idea: The word 'democracy' comes from the Greek 'demos' (people) and 'kratos' (rule/power), so it literally means 'rule of the people'. Since not all people can rule directly, India, like other modern democracies, is a representative democracy: citizens elect representatives -- MLAs (Members of Legislative Assembly) at the State level and MPs (Members of Parliament) at the national level -- who discuss laws, problems and solutions through dialogue and debate.
concepts.rule: Direct democracy is when every individual's own opinion is counted towards a decision (as in a class vote by a show of hands); representative democracy is when people instead elect representatives to decide on their behalf (as in a class electing a monitor to speak to the principal). Grassroots democracy refers to a system that enables and encourages the participation of ordinary citizens -- the base of the three-tier pyramid -- so they can have a say in decisions that affect them.
concepts.example: India is the world's largest democracy, with about 970 million voters in 2024, and in principle every Indian citizen above the age of 18 has the right to vote; a class voting by a show of hands on where to go for a picnic is an example of direct democracy, since every student's opinion is directly counted.

questions.a: In representative democracy, illustrated by the class electing a monitor to speak to the principal, people choose someone to make decisions or speak on their behalf, rather than doing so themselves. In direct democracy, illustrated by the class voting by a show of hands to choose between picnic places A and B, every individual's own opinion is counted directly in the decision. According to the chapter, India, like other modern democracies, is a representative democracy: citizens elect MLAs and MPs who discuss and decide on laws and problems on their behalf.
s: Explains representative democracy using the class-monitor example (a representative decides or acts on the group's behalf)
Explains direct democracy using the picnic example (every individual's opinion directly counted)
States that the chapter describes India as a representative democracy, electing MLAs and MPs

questions.q: The chapter defines grassroots democracy as being about ordinary citizens forming 'the base of the pyramid' shown in Fig. 10.4. Explain what this comparison to a pyramid's base suggests about the importance of ordinary citizens' participation.
questions.a: Fig. 10.4 shows local government at the base of the pyramid, with State and Central government above it; describing ordinary citizens' participation as this same 'base' suggests that grassroots-level participation is the foundation the rest of the democratic system rests on, so that decisions ultimately connect back to, and are shaped by, the people at the base, not only by those at the top.
s: Connects grassroots democracy to Local Government's position at the base of the Fig. 10.4 pyramid
Explains this suggests ordinary citizens' participation is a foundational part of the system, not a minor addition at the top

questions.q: A student argues, 'Since India is a representative democracy, ordinary citizens have no real say in decisions between elections.' Evaluate this claim using the chapter's discussion of grassroots democracy.
questions.a: This claim overstates the case. While it is true that India functions mainly as a representative democracy, with elected MLAs and MPs, the chapter also introduces grassroots democracy -- a system that enables and encourages the participation of ordinary citizens, so that they can have a say in decisions that affect them, not only through periodic elections. This suggests Indian democracy is not limited to voting alone; there is also a recognised space for citizens' more direct, ongoing participation, which the claim ignores.
s: Rejects or substantially qualifies the claim rather than accepting it outright
Explains that grassroots democracy is about ongoing citizen participation in decisions, not only elections
Concludes that Indian democracy therefore includes more than representative decision-making alone

questions.q: Design a short pledge (3 lines) for a new 'grassroots citizens' committee' in a neighbourhood, reflecting the chapter's definition of grassroots democracy and at least one other idea from the chapter (such as governance, rules, or representative democracy).
questions.a: Sample pledge: 'We pledge to give every resident of our neighbourhood, not just its elected representatives, a genuine say in decisions that affect our daily lives. We pledge to discuss our differences through dialogue, in the same spirit as elected members debate in their assemblies. We pledge to remember that good governance depends on ordinary citizens' participation, from the base of the pyramid upwards.'
s: Reflects the chapter's definition of grassroots democracy (participation of ordinary citizens in decisions affecting them)
Connects to at least one other chapter idea (governance, dialogue and debate in assemblies, or representative democracy)
The pledge is coherent and consistent with the chapter's own concepts, not contradicting them
